issues.issue: The provision cites "Section XDI", a section that does not exist in the Policy; the intended reference to Section XIII must be supplied by construction.

The retention figures in this Discovery Period table (e.g. $160,000 for Directors and Officers Liability) do not match the retentions set out in Item 9 of the Declarations ($0 / $100,000), leaving which retention governs Discovery Period Claims open.
"Financial Impairment" is defined in Section IV(I) solely as a status of the Company or a Subsidiary, yet this paragraph applies it to the acquiring entity, which is neither.

"The acquiring entity" is used with the definite article but is nowhere identified or defined, and the qualifier "only for Wrongful Acts involving the entity or entities set forth in Item 1" leaves the scope of that entity's coverage uncertain.
The stated expiration is written "0443/2009", which is not a date, so the end of the Policy Period cannot be read off the face of the item.

The $10,000,000 Total Policy Limit sits against Item 8, which sets separate Limits of Liability for five Insuring Agreements totalling more than $10,000,000, leaving the interaction of the aggregate cap and the individual limits to be worked out.

The footnote says Insuring Agreement (C) includes Securities Liability coverage and that a separate agreement is provided only if coverage is "excluded under Insuring Agreement (C)", yet the table also grants a separate $10,000,000 Securities Liability agreement, so the overlap with (C) must be construed.
Item 6 shows IRA/Keogh Liability as N/A with no limit or premium, while this item fixes a $5,000 retention for IRA/Keogh Claims, leaving it unclear whether such coverage exists at all.
The list of incorporated endorsements differs from the lists in the later Declarations amendments (c020 and c024), so which endorsements form part of the Policy is not settled by this item alone.

This clause makes the Declarations, Application, Policy and Endorsements the contract, while Section XVI(B) describes the entire agreement as the Policy, Application and written Endorsements without mentioning the Declarations.

The endorsement extending the Policy Period is made effective at 12:01 a.m. on 04/13/2009, the precise moment the previous Policy Period expired under Item 2, raising the question whether it operated before expiry.

Placing Vantus Bank first in Item 1 changes the identity of the "Named Insured" as defined in Section IV (the first named entity), which controls notice, cancellation and the Discovery Period election.

Coverage is conditioned on a limit, retention and premium being "set forth in the Declarations", yet Item 6 shows the retention for Insuring Agreement (A) as $0/N-A and gives (A) and (B) a single combined premium.
The carve-out "except for Loss the Company pays as indemnification" turns on actual payment, and its boundary against advanced but unreimbursed Defense Costs is not stated.

The closing sentence withdrawing coverage for "any loss arising from any act or omission by an Insured Person's estate, heirs, legal representatives, assigns, or spouse" is capable of being read to negate most of the grant it qualifies.

This clause confines the conversion trigger for the Discovery Period to Section XIII(C)(1)(b), while Section XIII(C)(2) states that the occurrence of any of the conversion events in (C)(1) — including Financial Impairment under (a) — shall not affect the right to purchase the Discovery Period.

The Discovery Period Activation endorsement lists separate amounts and premiums for each coverage, which sits awkwardly with this statement that the Discovery Period limit is part of and not in addition to the preceding Policy Year's limit.
"A written or oral demand for monetary damages or non-monetary relief" has no threshold of formality, so whether a letter, regulatory communication or informal demand is a Claim is genuinely open.

The Discovery Period Activation endorsement deletes and replaces this definition (c004) with one that adds "the acquiring entity" and drops the bank-Subsidiary limb, so two inconsistent definitions of Company appear in the instrument.
"Reasonable and necessary legal fees and expenses" is an undefined standard, and the exclusion of "overhead" has no stated boundary against billed disbursements.
"Leased Employee" and "Independent Contractor" are capitalised as defined terms, but Section IV contains no definition of either, so the carve-out from "Employee" has no stated content.

"Common nexus" with "any fact, circumstance, situation, event, transaction or series of related facts" sets no limit on how loose the connection may be, and it drives the single-Claim and prior-notice provisions.

The carve-outs from "Loss" — notably (3) "any unpaid, unrecoverable or outstanding loan, lease or extension of credit to any customer" and (6) depreciation of investment products "due to market fluctuation unrelated to any Wrongful Act" — collide with the general grant for amounts the Insureds are legally obligated to pay, so whether a lending or investment loss is recoverable "Loss" turns on which words control.

The definition fixes the Named Insured as the first entity in Item 1, but the Change of Name endorsement (c023) reordered Item 1 to put Vantus Bank first, so the identity of the Named Insured shifts mid-term.

"Pollutants include but are not limited to" a list of specific substances, leaving the reach of the open-ended category (and of "any solid, liquid, gaseous or thermal organism") to be fixed by construction.
Limb (1) requires ownership of "more than fifty percent (50%)" while limb (2) requires "fifty percent (50%) or more", so identically-sized holdings qualify or not depending on entity form.
Limb (5), "trustee exercising any other trust or fiduciary powers permitted by law", is a catch-all sitting against four detailed enumerations, so its reach beyond the listed roles is uncertain.

"While acting solely in the capacity as such" is the operative limit on covered acts, and "solely" gives no guidance where a director acts in mixed capacities (for example as director and shareholder).

The exclusion sweeps in "damage to or destruction of any tangible or intangible property", a phrase broad enough on one reading to bar ordinary economic-loss claims that the Insuring Agreements are meant to cover.
"Acting independently of, and totally without the solicitation, assistance, participation, or intervention of any Insured" gives no measure of what degree of contact defeats independence.

Limb (3), "any other violation of any statutory or common law relating to employment", is a general catch-all appended to two lists of specific employment wrongs, so how far it extends beyond them is open.

"Any pension, profit sharing or employee benefit program established in whole or in part for the benefit of Employees" is broad enough that its boundary against ordinary mismanagement claims is not fixed.

The exclusion covers property "acquired by the Company as security or collateral", while the exception restores Claims arising "in connection with the foreclosure process", and the line between the two is not drawn.

"Arising out of or in any way involving any fraudulent, dishonest or criminal act" is qualified by a final-adjudication proviso, leaving it contestable whether the exclusion bites on claims pleaded in both fraud and negligence.

Limb (3) excludes Loss involving "conflicts of interest, engaging in self-dealing, or acting in bad faith" with no adjudication requirement beyond the words "in fact", so what establishes the fact and how far the phrase reaches is open.

"Any Claim by, on behalf of, or at the behest of the Company" does not say whether a successor, receiver or assignee of the Company suing the Insured Persons is caught, and the three enumerated exceptions invite an expressio unius argument that no other claimant is excepted.

Read to bar every claim brought by anyone standing in the Company's shoes, the exclusion cannot easily be squared with Section XVI(I) (Insolvency/Bankruptcy), which preserves the Insurer's obligations on Financial Impairment, or with Section XIII(C)(1)(a), which keeps the Policy in force for pre-receivership Wrongful Acts.
"Any similar insurance policy providing protection for any Insured" fixes no test of similarity, and "any fact, circumstance or situation" noticed to another carrier is unbounded.

"The same or substantially the same fact, circumstance or situation underlying or alleged in such prior litigation" gives no measure of substantial sameness, which is the whole operation of the exclusion.
The exception "except as provided in Section XII (C)(3)" points to a subsection that does not exist: Section XII(C) contains only limbs (1) and (2), so the carve-back has no referent.

"Any insurance carrier or bond carrier of the Company" and "directly or indirectly by or for the benefit of" are undefined, so whether a claim by or for a deposit insurer or fidelity bond carrier is caught is arguable.

Excluding every Claim "involving the Financial Impairment of the Company or any Subsidiary" is hard to reconcile with Section XVI(I), which says Financial Impairment of the Insured shall not release the Insurer from its obligations, and with Section XIII(C)(1)(a), which keeps the Policy in force after a receiver is appointed.
Limb (6), "any other investment banking activity", is a general catch-all following five specific activities, so whether it is limited by the enumerated kinds is open to ejusdem generis argument.

"The Company's function or activity as receiver, trustee in bankruptcy, or assignee for the benefit of creditors" can be read either as the Company acting in those roles or as claims involving a receivership of the Company itself.
"The D&O Limit of Liability set forth in Item 8" uses a term the Policy never defines, and Item 8 sets out five different limits, so which figure caps each Insuring Agreement is not stated.
The reinstatement is tied to IRA/Keogh Claims under Insuring Agreement (C), but Item 6 of the Declarations lists IRA/Keogh Liability as N/A with no limit, retention or premium.

Whether the Company is "legally permitted or required to advance Defense Costs or indemnify", judged "regardless of whether actual indemnification is granted", is the operative test and is not defined by reference to any body of law.

The subsection first says the retentions for each affected Insuring Agreement are summed, then says the total retention "shall in no event exceed the largest of such applicable retentions", which cannot both be applied to the same Claim.

Deeming a single Claim first made on the earliest date "regardless of whether such date is before or during the Policy Period" pulls against Insuring Agreements (A)-(C), which cover only Claims "first made during the Policy Period or the Discovery Period".
The trigger is whether the limit "is a sublimit of the D&O Policy", but "D&O Policy" and "sublimit" are undefined and Item 7 (separate limit) is blank for every Insuring Agreement.

The order of payments is triggered only when, "in the Insurer's judgment", Loss "could reasonably exceed" the Total Policy Limit, a standard that mixes the Insurer's subjective view with an objective qualifier.

This subsection speaks of "Financial Impairment of the Company or any Insured Person", but Section IV(I) defines Financial Impairment only as a status of the Company or a Subsidiary, so it cannot attach to an Insured Person.

A flat bar on incurring any Defense Costs without prior written consent is difficult to square with Section IX(A)(1), which places the duty to defend on the Insured, and with Section IX(B)(1), which obliges the Insurer to advance Defense Costs currently.
Notice must be given "as soon as practicable" yet also within a fixed sixty days, so whether late-but-within-sixty-days notice breaches the condition precedent is left open.
The condition precedent that notice "be specific and contain full particulars" including "the causes of action to be asserted" sets no measurable threshold for a notice of circumstances.

This subsection sets the acquisition threshold at twenty-five percent (25%) of total assets, while Endorsement 2223 (c195) deletes and replaces Section XII(A) with a 20% threshold, so two figures for the same trigger appear in the instrument.
Automatic coverage is given for banks with assets "less than twenty-five percent (25%)" of total assets, whereas Endorsement 2223 (c196) replaces the same subsection with a 20% figure.

Excluding every Claim resulting from Wrongful Acts "committed prior to the effective date of such acquisition, merger or creation" largely empties Section XII(B), which promises automatic coverage for an acquired bank and its Insured Persons.

The Named Insured's right to cancel and recover unearned premium cannot be squared with Section XIII(C)(2), which states that on a conversion event the Policy "may not be cancelled and the entire premium shall be deemed fully earned".

The Iowa Amendatory Endorsement (c200) deletes and replaces this same Section XIII(B)(1) with a version that permits cancellation only for six enumerated reasons, so two inconsistent cancellation regimes sit in the instrument.

A promise to return 100% of unearned premium on Insurer cancellation pulls against Section XIII(C)(2) and Section III, which deem the entire premium fully earned on conversion and on Discovery Period activation.
"The Company ceasing to engage actively in its primary business" fixes no test for when active engagement ends, yet it cuts off all coverage for subsequent Wrongful Acts.

Only limb (b) of this subsection is picked up in Section III as a conversion that entitles the Insured to purchase the Discovery Period, although Section XIII(C)(2) says the occurrence of any of these events shall not affect that right.

The statement that the Policy "may not be cancelled and the entire premium shall be deemed fully earned" contradicts Section XIII(A) and (B), which give both the Named Insured and the Insurer cancellation rights with return of unearned premium.
"Relative legal exposures of the parties" is an undefined allocation yardstick with no method, timing or decision-maker specified.

Allocation between covered and uncovered Loss "based on the relative legal exposures of the Insureds" supplies no measure, and this is the classic point at which insurer and insured read the same words differently.
"Best efforts to reach a proper allocation" states neither what efforts suffice nor what makes an allocation "proper".
The Insurer need advance only those Defense Costs "which the Insurer believes to be covered", a purely subjective trigger for an interim payment obligation.
Arbitration binds only if "requested by the Insured", so the clause is mandatory for the Insurer and optional for the Insured, and whether it is a condition precedent to suit is unstated.

Treating the Application as "a separate Application for coverage by each Insured Person" sits uneasily with the very next subsection (c134), which denies that the Policy is a series of individual insurance contracts.

Denying that the Policy is "a series of individual insurance contracts" pulls against Section XV(A)(1) (separate Application per Insured Person) and Section XV(C)(1) (no imputation of knowledge between Insured Persons), which both presuppose insured-by-insured treatment.

Conditioning forfeiture on an Insured Person "who knew of any fact ... not truthfully disclosed" is contradicted by the following sentence (c137), which applies the same conditions "whether or not the Insured Person actually knew".

The sentence "whether or not the Insured Person actually knew if the misrepresentation or untruthful disclosure was made" is ungrammatical and its object is unclear, changing whether knowledge matters at all.
It cannot be reconciled with the severability clause it qualifies (c136), which withholds coverage only from an Insured Person who knew of the undisclosed fact.
The entire-agreement list (Policy, Application, written Endorsements) omits the Declarations, which the Declarations page itself (c018) makes part of the contract.
Making the "Named Insured" the agent for all Insureds depends on Section IV's definition of Named Insured as the first entity in Item 1, which the Change of Name endorsement (c023) altered mid-term.
"Full compliance with all the terms of this Policy" as a condition precedent to any action gives no allowance for immaterial or non-prejudicial breach, and its reach is not stated.

Making this Policy excess to "any other existing insurance regardless of whether collectable" while also declaring it "not subject to the terms of any other insurance" leaves the priority rule uncertain against another policy with its own excess clause.

The promise that Financial Impairment of the Insured "shall not release the Insurer from its obligations" is difficult to reconcile with the Insolvency Exclusion (Section VI(D)(1)), which bars Loss for any Claim involving the Financial Impairment of the Company.

Excluding all Claims involving securities issued by the Company, subject only to a carve-out for Form 5098, cuts across Item 6 of the Declarations, whose footnote states that Insuring Agreement (C) includes Securities Liability coverage.
Limb (6), "any other investment banking activity", is an open-ended catch-all following five specific activities, leaving its scope to ejusdem generis argument.
The exclusion reaches "actual or written representations", a phrase that makes no sense as written (evidently "oral or written"), so whether unwritten statements are caught is uncertain.

"The Company's function or activity as receiver, trustee in bankruptcy, or assignee for the benefit of creditors" can be read as the Company acting in those roles or as claims involving a receivership over the Company.

The definition brings in plans "acquired during the Policy Period pursuant to Section XII", but Section XII deals with acquisitions of entities and says nothing about benefit plans, and it is deleted outright by the Discovery Period Activation endorsement.

Limb (2) excludes "criminal or civil fines or penalties imposed by law" while the closing sentence says Loss "shall not exclude" specified ERISA civil penalties, so the two statements must be reconciled by construction.

"Any Claim by, on behalf of, or at the behest of the Company" does not say whether a successor or receiver suing in the Company's right is caught, and the four enumerated exceptions invite an expressio unius reading.
The exclusion repeatedly turns on "other Employee Program", a capitalised term that neither the Fiduciary endorsement nor Section IV of the Policy defines.
As printed the clause reads that the Insurer "shall be liable", omitting the negative that the whole exclusion depends on.

The grant covers Wrongful Acts "which in whole or in part is based upon, arises from, or is in consequence of" a securities transaction, and the "in part" language leaves the boundary against non-securities claims uncertain.

Excluding Claims involving the "Financial Impairment of the Company" from the Securities Liability coverage is hard to square with Section XVI(I), which says the Insured's Financial Impairment does not release the Insurer from its obligations.
Limb (6), "any other investment banking activity", is a general catch-all appended to five specific activities, leaving its reach beyond them open.

"The Company's function or activity as receiver, trustee in bankruptcy, or assignee for the benefit of creditors" is capable of being read either as the Company acting in those roles or as claims involving a receivership over the Company.
This subsection purports to delete and replace Section XVI(J) but reproduces it word for word, so the only operative change is the added exclusivity sentence that follows it.

Making Securities Liability coverage exclusive of "any other Insuring Agreement" contradicts Section VII(A)(3), which expressly contemplates a Claim subject to more than one Insuring Agreement, and Section VIII(B), which orders payments across Insuring Agreements for the same Claim.

This replacement sets the acquisition threshold at 20% of total assets whereas the printed Section XII(A)(2) in the policy form (c115) says twenty-five percent (25%), leaving two thresholds in the instrument for the same trigger.
The 20% automatic-coverage threshold conflicts on its face with the twenty-five percent (25%) figure in the printed Section XII(B) (c116).
Sub-paragraph (c) is introduced by four roman numerals but is followed by six separate cancellation grounds, so which grounds are enumerated under it cannot be read off the text.
This endorsement replaces Section XIII(B)(1), yet the unamended text remains in the policy form (c119) allowing cancellation "for any other reason" on sixty days' notice.
